add_devices.title: Add discovered devices
add_devices.description: These devices have been seen since Home Assistant last started and are ready to add. Ignoring one hides it until you un-ignore it under "Ignored devices". Anything you leave unselected stays in this list and is offered again next time it is seen. Each entry shows how many times the device has been received, its signal level when it reports one, and how long ago it last transmitted. A device received once, weakly, is usually a bad decode or a neighbour's sensor.

data_description.add: The devices to create in Home Assistant.
data_description.ignore: The devices to hide. They stay hidden until you un-ignore them.

ignored_devices.title: Ignored devices
ignored_devices.description: These devices are hidden from the discovered-devices list. Select any you want offered again. A device reappears the next time it transmits, which for a door or motion sensor means the next time it is triggered.

data_description.unignore: The devices to offer again the next time they transmit.

data_description.availability_timeout: Mark a device unavailable after this many seconds without an event. Use 0 to never mark devices unavailable. Leave this at the default and each device type is handled automatically: devices that send only rare events (door, window, motion, doorbell) are never marked unavailable, while periodic sensors use 600 seconds. Set a specific value to apply it to every device instead.

device_settings.title: Device settings
device_settings.description: Settings for {device}. Leave the timeout blank to clear the override and use the receiver default. For a utility meter, choose a commodity to calibrate its consumption sensor for the Energy dashboard.

data_description.timeout_override: Mark this device unavailable after this many seconds without an event. Use 0 to never mark it unavailable. Leave blank to use the automatic default for this device's type (longer for door/window/motion sensors).

mappings.title: Device mappings
mappings.description: Add or correct this receiver's device-library mappings as YAML, using the same schema as the shipped library. See [how to write mappings]({docs_url}) for the format, examples, and how to scope an override to one device model. {problems}

calibration.title: Calibrate consumption ({commodity})
calibration.description: Set the base unit one raw consumption count represents and the scale applied to the counter. The sensor reports raw count x scale in this unit; Home Assistant converts to your preferred display unit. Changing this rebuilds the sensor and starts fresh long-term statistics.

data_description.unit: The unit one consumption count represents (before scale). Home Assistant converts between compatible units for display.
data_description.scale: Multiplier applied to the raw counter (for example 0.1 if each count is a tenth of a unit). Use 1 if each count is exactly one base unit.

replace.title: Replace device
replace.description: Some sensors generate a new transmitter id when their batteries are changed, so the same hardware turns up as a brand-new device. Pick the device you want to keep: its history, settings and automations are moved onto the new id.

data_description.device: The existing device whose history you want to preserve.

replace_target.title: Replace device
replace_target.description: Pick the newly seen device that is really the same hardware as {device}. Devices you have not added are listed too, marked "not added yet" with how often they have been received. After a battery change the replacement is usually one of those. Any duplicate entities are removed and the device you kept takes over its id. Devices of the same model are listed first.

data_description.device: The device that appeared after the batteries were changed. It does not need to be added first.

sample_rate_low_for_band.title: rtl_433 sample rate may be low for this frequency: {title}

init.title: Sample rate may be too low
init.description:
The radio on {title} is tuned to a high-band frequency but is still sampling at the bare default rate. rtl_433 does not widen the sample rate automatically when it is retuned, so devices in the upper ISM bands may decode poorly.

- **Increase the sample rate** sets the **Sample rate** to {suggested} Hz — the 1.024 MS/s rate rtl_433 itself uses by default.
- **Keep the current rate** leaves the rate unchanged and stops this advisory from appearing again for this receiver. Many devices still decode fine at the lower rate, so this is a valid choice.

menu_options.ignore: Keep the current rate (don't warn again)

confirm.title: Event timestamps cannot be read
confirm.description:
Events from {title} carry no timestamp this integration can read, so it cannot tell a freshly received transmission from one the server is re-sending.

rtl_433 re-broadcasts a short buffer of recent events every time Home Assistant reconnects. Without usable timestamps those are treated as new traffic: devices that have actually gone silent are marked available again, and their event entities and device triggers fire a second time — which can re-run automations.

To fix it, add `report_meta time:iso:usec:tz` to the rtl_433 configuration (or start it with `-M time:iso:usec:tz`) and restart the server. This card clears itself once timestamps start arriving.

Submit to acknowledge this and stop the warning for this receiver — choose this if you deliberately run without timestamps.
